title: Enchanting African Teardrop Cascade Mehndi Design for Finger
descriptionParagraphs: A classic african mehndi design designed for the fingers, featuring wave pattern and star cluster. Rated as Medium, this pattern is perfect for Eid.

Finger designs are quick to apply and dry fast, which makes them practical when time is short. Fingertips have thicker skin, so the stain there usually develops darker than on the rest of the hand. This pattern suits someone who is already comfortable with basic lines, dots and petals and wants to practise even spacing.

Henna has been worn across North, West and East Africa for centuries, with distinct styles in countries such as Sudan, Mali, Mauritania and Somalia. In Sudan, henna is closely tied to weddings, and brides traditionally wear bold, dark designs on both hands and feet.

Application tips: Bold African-style designs need a thicker line, so cut the cone tip slightly wider than you would for fine work. For solid filled areas, apply an even layer of paste; thin patches stain lighter than the rest.

faq.q: What makes African henna designs different?
faq.a: They favour bold lines, solid fills and geometric shapes over the fine floral detail common in Indian mehndi, and the look varies a lot between regions.

faq.q: How is the tape technique used in West African henna?
faq.a: Thin strips of tape are placed on the skin in a pattern, henna is applied over the whole area, and the tape is removed after the paste dries to reveal sharp unstained lines.

faq.q: Is African henna only worn at weddings?
faq.a: No. It is also worn for Eid, naming ceremonies and other family celebrations, usually in simpler designs than bridal henna.

title: Charming African Lotus Pattern Mehndi Design for Back Hand
descriptionParagraphs: A stunning african mehndi design tailored for the back of the hand, featuring bracelet cuff and ring pattern. Rated as Expert, this pattern is perfect for a party.

Skin on the back of the hand is thinner than the palm, so the stain is usually lighter and fades sooner. Leaving the paste on for longer helps the colour develop. This is a detailed pattern usually done by an experienced artist; allow plenty of time and work in small sections.

In Mali and Mauritania, artists often lay thin strips of tape on the skin and apply henna over them, which leaves crisp geometric lines when the tape is removed. In Hausa-speaking communities of Nigeria and Niger, henna is known as lalle and is worn for weddings and festivals.
Application tips: Use strips of tape or a stencil to keep long straight edges clean. Leave the paste on for at least four to six hours; the longer it stays, the deeper the stain.
